name: Time as 'the moving image of eternity'
plain_explanation: Because the created world could not be made literally eternal like its perfect model, God instead gave it time -- a kind of moving, numbered copy of changeless eternity -- and time and the heavens came into being at the very same instant.
precise_definition: Plato's account of time as a created 'moving image of eternity,' proceeding 'according to number,' brought into existence simultaneously with the heavens, such that strictly speaking one should say only 'is' of eternal being, while 'was' and 'will be' properly apply to the created, temporal image of eternity.
why_it_mattered: It is one of the earliest sustained philosophical treatments of the relationship between time and eternity, later echoed in medieval theology's distinction between God's timeless eternity and the created world's temporal duration.
historical_origin: Original to the Timaeus, though building on the eternal/changing distinction basic to Plato's whole philosophy.
examples: 'He resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order the heaven, he made this image eternal but moving according to number... and this image we call Time.'
God made the sun 'so that animals could learn arithmetic' -- the succession of day and night, Plato suggests, is what first gave rise to the very concept of number.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes the English poet Henry Vaughan seems to echo this passage in the line 'I saw eternity the other night.'
